text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is officially considered to start when your readings are consistently at or above 130 mm Hg for the top number (systolic) or 80 mm Hg for the bottom number (diastolic), according to guidelines from the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

snippet_highlighted_words: consistently at or above 130 mm Hg for the top number (systolic) or 80 mm Hg for the bottom number (diastolic)

text_blocks.snippet: Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) using two numbers: systolic (pressure when your heart beats) over diastolic (pressure when your heart rests between beats).

list.snippet: Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 1 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic
Stage 2 Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic (requires immediate medical attention)
Stage 1: Doctors typically recommend lifestyle changes and may evaluate your overall heart disease or stroke risk to see if medication is needed.
Stage 2: Doctors usually prescribe a combination of lifestyle changes and blood pressure medication.

Hypertensive Emergency (>180/120 mm Hg with symptoms): If your reading is this high and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or vision changes, call 911 immediately. If your reading is over 180/120 mm Hg without symptoms, rest for five minutes and recheck; if it remains high, contact your healthcare provider right away.
